swift-ats-allow-arbitrary-loads.problem: NSAllowsArbitraryLoads disables App Transport Security entirely. Your app can then make plaintext HTTP requests, and TLS misconfigurations on remote servers are accepted without complaint.
swift-ats-allow-arbitrary-loads.impact: Network traffic can be read or modified on hostile networks (public Wi-Fi, hotel proxies). Apple App Store review also flags this and may reject the binary.
swift-ats-allow-arbitrary-loads.fix: Remove NSAllowsArbitraryLoads. If a specific domain truly requires HTTP, declare a narrow exception in NSExceptionDomains with the smallest possible scope.

swift-http-cleartext-url.problem: URL(string: "http://...") creates an unencrypted endpoint. ATS will block the request on iOS 9+, and even when it works, the data is visible to anyone on the same network.
swift-http-cleartext-url.impact: Credentials, tokens, and personal data sent over this URL can be intercepted or tampered with.
swift-http-cleartext-url.fix: Switch the URL to https://. If the server does not support TLS, fix the server — do not weaken the client.

swift-userdefaults-secret.problem: UserDefaults stores values in a plist file inside the app sandbox in plaintext. On a jailbroken device or via iTunes/Files backup, anyone with access to that file can read the secret.
swift-userdefaults-secret.impact: Authentication tokens, passwords, and API keys are exposed across reboots and accessible to forensic tools.
swift-userdefaults-secret.fix: Use the Keychain Services API (SecItemAdd / KeychainSwift / SwiftKeychainWrapper) with an appropriate kSecAttrAccessible value.

swift-hardcoded-api-key.problem: Embedding a long string secret in source code means the value ends up in the compiled binary. `strings YourApp` or any disassembler will recover it in seconds.
swift-hardcoded-api-key.impact: Anyone who downloads your app from the App Store can extract the secret and reuse it from outside your app.
swift-hardcoded-api-key.fix: Load the secret from a server-issued token after authentication, or store it in the Keychain after a one-time setup. For build-time config, use xcconfig files excluded from the repository.

swift-weak-crypto-md5.problem: MD5 is broken for any security purpose — collisions can be produced in seconds on commodity hardware.
swift-weak-crypto-md5.impact: Signatures, integrity checks, and password hashes built on MD5 can be forged or precomputed by attackers.
swift-weak-crypto-md5.fix: Use SHA-256 from CryptoKit (SHA256.hash(data:)) for integrity, and Argon2/bcrypt/scrypt or PBKDF2 for password hashing.

swift-weak-crypto-sha1.problem: SHA-1 collisions have been publicly demonstrated. It must not be used for digital signatures, certificates, or any tamper-evident purpose.
swift-weak-crypto-sha1.impact: An attacker can craft two different inputs that share the same SHA-1 hash, defeating integrity checks.
swift-weak-crypto-sha1.fix: Use SHA-256 (or SHA-512) from CryptoKit. For HMAC, use HMAC<SHA256> from CryptoKit.

swift-keychain-no-access-control.problem: SecItemAdd called without kSecAttrAccessControl means the Keychain item uses default access — typically accessible whenever the device is unlocked, with no biometric or device-passcode requirement.
swift-keychain-no-access-control.impact: If the device is unlocked and handed to someone (or compromised by another app exploiting an OS bug), the secret can be read without further authentication.
swift-keychain-no-access-control.fix: Add a kSecAttrAccessControl with SecAccessControlCreateWithFlags using .userPresence, .biometryCurrentSet, or .devicePasscode depending on your threat model.

swift-webview-js-enabled.problem: Enabling JavaScript on a WKWebView is only safe if every URL ever loaded is under your control. If untrusted HTML or a redirect can reach this view, JS becomes an XSS surface.
swift-webview-js-enabled.impact: An attacker controlling the loaded content can call native bridges, read DOM data, or pivot to other origins via redirects.
swift-webview-js-enabled.fix: Disable JS unless required (configuration.defaultWebpagePreferences.allowsContentJavaScript = false), and restrict loads to a fixed allowlist of trusted origins.

swift-webview-load-untrusted-html.problem: loadHTMLString with baseURL: nil renders the HTML as if it were a local file. Any <script> in $STR runs in your app's web context with no Same-Origin Policy enforcement.
swift-webview-load-untrusted-html.impact: If $STR includes user input, you have stored XSS inside your own app, which can call JS bridges and exfiltrate data.
swift-webview-load-untrusted-html.fix: HTML-escape user input before injecting it into the string, or render markdown/text in native UIKit/SwiftUI views instead of a webview.

swift-eval-via-nsexpression.problem: NSExpression parses and evaluates the format string at runtime, including function calls and arithmetic. If the format contains anything user-controlled, the user can run code.
swift-eval-via-nsexpression.impact: Attackers can invoke arbitrary selectors, leading to crashes or, with clever use of FUNCTION(), real code execution.
swift-eval-via-nsexpression.fix: Never build the format string from user input. Use a small custom parser, or compute the value in Swift code directly.

swift-trust-all-cert.problem: Calling completionHandler(.useCredential, URLCredential(trust: trust)) in didReceive challenge accepts the server certificate regardless of validity. This neuters TLS.
swift-trust-all-cert.impact: Any network adversary (corporate proxy, café Wi-Fi, hostile router) can intercept and modify HTTPS traffic.
swift-trust-all-cert.fix: Either let the system do default validation (call completionHandler(.performDefaultHandling, nil)) or pin the certificate/public key explicitly with SecTrustEvaluateWithError.

swift-print-sensitive.problem: print() writes to the unified system log without privacy redaction. Anything you print is visible in Console.app while the device is connected to a Mac.
swift-print-sensitive.impact: Tokens, user IDs, or PII printed during debugging may stay in production builds and leak via device logs.
swift-print-sensitive.fix: Use os.Logger with privacy modifiers — logger.info("user \(id, privacy: .private)") — and gate verbose logs behind #if DEBUG.

swift-runtime-shell-exec.problem: Process().arguments accepts an array of strings sent to a subprocess. If any element is built from user input without strict validation, the user can change which program runs or pass arbitrary flags.
swift-runtime-shell-exec.impact: Command injection on macOS-side tooling — leads to code execution as the current user.
swift-runtime-shell-exec.fix: Validate every argument against an allowlist before passing it, and never pass user input as the executable path.

swift-deeplink-no-validation.problem: The application(_:open:options:) handler receives a URL but the body never inspects url.scheme or url.host. Any app on the device can open your scheme and trigger any code path you wire up.
swift-deeplink-no-validation.impact: A malicious app can craft a deep link to log the user out, transfer state, or open privileged screens.
swift-deeplink-no-validation.fix: Check url.scheme matches your registered scheme and url.host matches an expected route, reject otherwise. Treat URL parameters as untrusted input.

swift-force-unwrap.problem: The postfix ! operator unwraps an Optional and crashes the process if the value is nil. Crashes from force-unwraps are one of the most common causes of iOS app crashes.
swift-force-unwrap.impact: A nil value produces an EXC_BREAKPOINT and an immediate crash visible to the user.
swift-force-unwrap.fix: Use `if let` / `guard let`, the `??` nil-coalescing operator, or optional chaining. Reserve ! for values that are provably non-nil by construction.

swift-force-try.problem: try! ignores the do/catch contract and crashes the process if the call throws.
swift-force-try.impact: Any thrown error — including ones a user can trigger (bad file, network issue) — becomes a hard crash.
swift-force-try.fix: Wrap the call in do/catch and handle the error, or use `try?` to convert it to an Optional when you can recover with nil.

swift-empty-catch.problem: An empty catch block silently swallows the error. The program continues as if nothing happened, which makes failures invisible until they cause data corruption downstream.
swift-empty-catch.impact: Bugs hide for a long time, and incident debugging is much harder without the original error.
swift-empty-catch.fix: At minimum log the error (Logger / os_log). Better, decide whether the function should rethrow, return a Result, or fall back to a safe default.

swift-todo-comment.problem: TODO and FIXME comments are reminders that something is incomplete or broken. They tend to accumulate and get forgotten over time.
swift-todo-comment.impact: Tracked technical debt drifts; comments alone do not get triaged or scheduled.
swift-todo-comment.fix: Either fix the item immediately or open a ticket in your tracker and reference its ID in the comment, then remove the bare TODO.

swift-fatalError-prod.problem: fatalError() unconditionally crashes the app. It is appropriate for code paths that should be impossible, but not for input validation or unexpected runtime state.
swift-fatalError-prod.impact: A reachable fatalError gives users a hard crash where graceful handling would be possible.
swift-fatalError-prod.fix: Replace with proper error propagation (throw, Result), an assertion (assertionFailure only crashes in debug builds), or a UI error state.
